thread.title: Jeffrey Gundlach says stocks still haven't hit a 'panic low'

author: morningstar.com
title: Jeffrey Gundlach says stocks still haven't hit a 'panic low'
text:
By Barbara Kollmeyer, MarketWatch
Critical information for the U.S. trading day
A Thanksgiving getaway from this stock market perhaps never sounded so good.
A bit of a bounce looks to be building for Wednesday's session. But some investors may be wary of what could be a classic dead-cat howler, especially with many traders out until Monday.
(https://twitter.com/KeithMcCullough/status/1065187903544922112)
The topic du jour is where stocks go from now, and everyone has an opinion
DoubleLine Capital's top dog Jeffrey Gundlach told Reuters (https://www.reuters.com/article/us-funds-doubleline-idUSKCN1NP2EB?utm_campaign=trueAnthem:+Trending+Content&utm_content=5bf4cc8b04d3015276cb00e3&utm_medium=trueAnthem&utm_source=twitter) that the selloff will continue and we aren't yet seeing "anything resembling a panic low." Now is the time for "capital preservation," said Gundlach, adding that investors should steer clear of investment-grade bonds for one.
Some credited Gundlach's comments with triggering a near 650-point drop at one point for the Dow on Tuesday.
There's an echo of Gundlach's advice in our first call of the day from Morgan Stanley's chief investment officer Mike Wilson who told CNBC Tuesday (https://www.cnbc.com/video/2018/11/20/dont-buy-this-dip-says-morgan-stanleys-top-strategist.html) that it is too soon to buy into this latest dip.
"It all stems back to liquidity and the Fed and the tightening of financial conditions--that is our thesis all year--it's been this rolling bear market and we finally got to the big tech stocks. I actually think we're about 90% of the way done with the valuation damage that is going to happen," added Wilson.
The selloff is coming now because some investors are realizing that companies will be delivering some bad earnings news next year, Wilson said. He also wants to see some more dovish Fed comments.
Wilson is a cool cucumber, though saying the asset correction is a "normal course of business that is very natural at the end of a bull market that needs to consolidate." He's got his eye on cyclicals such as utilities, health care, energy and banks, because they've already discounted a lot of bad news. "They'll be the first to recover," he says.
Last word goes to our counter call of the day, from UBS's chief investment office, which sent a note to clients late Tuesday. "We view the selloff as overdone and a bull market correction, with valuations that have become more compelling," said UBS, adding that risk-reward for owning equities is "asymmetric to the upside over the next six months."
But they also hold so-called countercyclical positions, such as an overweight in 10-year U.S. Treasurys to manage market volatility as investors wait around for "more clarity on trade, the Fed and growth."

The market
Dow , S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures are pointing higher, though there's a way to go to make up for Tuesday's (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/dow-futures-tumble-nearly-300-points-nasdaq-poised-to-fall-by-triple-digits-2018-11-20) brutal session, in which the S&P and Dow erased 2018 gains, with a nasty fall for the Nasdaq as well.
Crude is also trying to recoup (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/oil-pauses-sharp-plunge-as-us-inventories-fall-but-saudi-output-under-close-watch-2018-11-21) some of Tuesday's sharp drop, while the dollar is down and gold is barely higher.

A bounce has extended to Europe , while Asia had a mixed session (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/asian-markets-continue-to-retreat-as-tech-stocks-get-hit-hard-2018-11-20), with some green for China .
The chart
Putting crude's 7% drop on Tuesday and miserable week in context is our chart of the day, which comes from Pension Partner's director Charlie Bilello. He tweeted this chart out that shows the biggest oil declines in history--a 77% drop between 2011 and 2016 so far is the winner:
(https://twitter.com/charliebilello/status/1065120460898295808)
The buzz
Deere (DE) is slumping after earnings fell short (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/deere-to-raise-prices-cut-costs-2018-08-17), and the tractor maker said it would lift prices and cut costs. And there was more bad news on the retail front with Gap (GPS) posting a 7% fall in comparable sales (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/gap-looks-to-close-hundreds-of-stores-2018-11-20) and exploring closure of hundreds of stores.
Read:Red Tuesday for retailers as Target's stock suffers worst stretch since financial crisis (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/red-tuesday-for-retailers-as-targets-stock-suffers-worst-stretch-since-the-financial-crisis-2018-11-20)
Apple's (AAPL) iPhone assembler Foxconn (2354.TW) is reportedly planning $2.9 billion in cost cuts as it faces a "very difficult and competitive year." (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/iphone-maker-foxconn-to-cut-29-billion-in-costs-in-2019-bloomberg-2018-11-21)
Despite a rocky year for the social-media group, Facebook (FB) CEO Mark Zuckerberg says he won't step down as chairman (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/zuckerberg-says-no-plan-to-step-down-as-facebook-chairman-2018-11-20) (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/zuckerberg-says-no-plan-to-step-down-as-facebook-chairman-2018-11-20) and threw his support behind COO Sheryl Sandberg amid criticism of her handling of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
U.S. trade rep Robert Lighthizer slams China (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/china-continues-unfair-trade-practices-says-us-trade-representative-2018-11-20) for "unfair, unreasonable and market-distorting" trade practices in a 50-page report on that country's trade practices.
The EU has rejected Italy's rule-busting budget proposal and says it is ready to slap down sanctions (https://www.cnbc.com/2018/11/21/eu-opens-disciplinary-procedures-against-italy.html).
Cybershopping next Monday? Avoid buying this stuff (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/6-things-not-to-buy-on-cyber-monday-2017-11-20).
The economy
It's the pre-Thanksgiving data dump: weekly jobless claims, durable goods orders are coming early, with existing-home sales, consumer sentiment and leading economic indicators to follow.
On the central-bank beat, Minneapolis Fed president and super dove Neil Kashkari said it is time to stop hiking rates (http://www.wbur.org/npr/669482149/its-time-to-stop-raising-interest-rates-kashkari-says). (http://www.wbur.org/npr/669482149/its-time-to-stop-raising-interest-rates-kashkari-says) And Jeremy Siegel, Wharton School finance professor, expects the Fed to definitely cut back on its hiking plans next year (https://www.cnbc.com/2018/11/20/jeremy-siegel-the-fed-could-substantially-ease-rate-hikes-in-2019.html?__source=twitter%7Cmain).
